headline: High-risk shared filesystem and broad egress make prompt injection, data leakage, and cascading errors plausible; Kestra’s workflow actions amplify impact.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: gpt-engineer writes files in a project directory and has no self-isolation by default; kestra reads/writes files and runs declarative workflows. That shared filesystem bridge makes attacker-controlled content from one agent plausibly influence the other, though no MCP or clipboard bridge is shown.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same project directory or mounted workspace
IF kestra ingests files produced by gpt-engineer as workflow inputs without provenance checks
mitigations: Use separate directories for each agent
Add a manual review step before kestra consumes any gpt-engineer output
Disable automatic file pickup from shared folders
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging to generated files

B_data_leakage.rationale: Both agents have broad network egress and filesystem access, and gpt-engineer explicitly handles OPENAI_API_KEY while kestra can process logs, inputs, variables, artifacts, and cloud data. A shared workspace can expose generated code or secrets to either agent’s backend, so leakage is plausible in default setups.
conditions: IF the two agents share a workspace containing secrets, logs, or artifacts
IF either agent uploads file contents from that workspace to its model or external services
mitigations: Keep secrets out of the shared project directory
Restrict network egress for one agent during review
Rotate any exposed API keys immediately
Separate logs/artifacts from code-generation outputs
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent workspace ACLs

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can execute shell commands, spawn subprocesses, read and write files, and kestra may also use root and docker.sock. With shared project-directory state and no locking described, concurrent writes can corrupt files or trigger unsafe actions; the overlap is dangerous by default.
conditions: IF both agents run against the same directory or repository
IF kestra tasks modify files while gpt-engineer is also writing generated code
mitigations: Run only one agent at a time on a given workspace
Use separate git branches or directories
Pause kestra writes while gpt-engineer is generating
requires-engineering: add file locking around shared state
requires-engineering: remove root/docker.sock from kestra

D_cascading_error.rationale: gpt-engineer produces code and offers to run it, while kestra executes declarative workflows and can trigger emails, cloud actions, and other side effects. If kestra treats gpt-engineer output as authoritative, a bad generation can cascade into irreversible downstream actions without verification.
conditions: IF kestra consumes gpt-engineer output as workflow definitions or task parameters
IF those workflows trigger external side effects such as email, cloud, or database actions
mitigations: Require human approval before executing generated workflows
Validate generated files against a schema before import
Run a dry-run mode first
Limit kestra to non-production targets
requires-engineering: add verification gates between agents

E_compliance.rationale: gpt-engineer touches generated source code and may handle an OpenAI API key, while kestra touches logs, inputs, variables, artifacts, database data, cloud storage data, and notifications. The profiles do not show residency or retention controls, so mixed handling of operational data creates a compliance mismatch risk, though not enough for a higher severity.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into kestra workflows or gpt-engineer prompts
IF retention or residency requirements differ between the two systems
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of both agents
Review retention settings before use
Document data flows for logs and artifacts
Use synthetic data for testing
requires-engineering: align residency and retention policies
